{\LARGE\bfseries\sffamily\color{AtlasNavy} First-order stationarity of nonconvex functions with only gradient smoothness and exact values\par}\vspace{5pt}


\textbf{Setting ID.} \texttt{SO\_\allowbreak{}ZO\_\allowbreak{}C01\_\allowbreak{}smooth\_\allowbreak{}only}



Single-objective optimization



Find an approximate first-order stationary point of the population objective \AtlasInlineMath{f}: an output point with sufficiently small gradient norm. The mathematical object is \AtlasInlineMath{\nabla f}, and information is acquired through the zeroth-order interface specified below.



\textbf{Status.} Other quantified gap



\textbf{TASK tags.} formulation: First order stationarity; solution concept: First order stationarity; task family: Single objective



\textbf{MODEL tags.} convexity: Convexity not assumed; initialization: Global initial gap; smoothness: Lipschitz gradient



\textbf{ORACLE tags.} access order: Zeroth-order interface; interface family: Exact value; public information: Public inputs explicitly declared; query domain: Full space



\textbf{ALGORITHMS tags.} adaptivity: Adaptive; randomization: Deterministic; randomization: Private randomness allowed; restriction: No additional span restriction explicitly imposed



\textbf{OUTPUT tags.} certificate: No additional output certificate required



\textbf{METRIC tags.} criterion: First order stationarity



\textbf{GUARANTEE tags.} aggregation: Per instance; mode: Deterministic; mode: Probability



\textbf{RESOURCE tags.} budget: Fixed worst-case budget



\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{1. Setting specification}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Task}


Find an approximate first-order stationary point of the population objective \AtlasInlineMath{f}: an output point with sufficiently small gradient norm. The mathematical object is \AtlasInlineMath{\nabla f}, and information is acquired through the zeroth-order interface specified below.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Admissible model}


\AtlasInlineMath{f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}} is differentiable and satisfies \AtlasInlineMath{\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2\le\beta\|x-y\|_2} for every \AtlasInlineMath{x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d}.



\AtlasInlineMath{f_*:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)>-\infty}, and the given initial point \AtlasInlineMath{x_0} satisfies \AtlasInlineMath{f(x_0)-f_*\le\Delta}.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Oracle interface}


At any finite query point \AtlasInlineMath{x} in \AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{R}^d}, the oracle returns the single exact scalar \AtlasInlineMath{f(x)}. The reply is uniquely determined and contains no gradient, subgradient or derivative-vector product.



The public inputs are \AtlasInlineMath{d}, \AtlasInlineMath{\beta}, \AtlasInlineMath{\Delta}, \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}, \AtlasInlineMath{x_0}, together with the sets, kernels and auxiliary operations explicitly declared above. Information about the unknown objective and any undisclosed sample distribution is obtained only through the stated interface.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Output}


Return \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{x}\in \mathbb{R}^d}. The output may be an unqueried point, an average or convex combination that remains in the stated space. No function value, gradient, inner solution, or accuracy certificate must accompany the output.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Loss or accuracy criterion}


The base loss is \AtlasInlineMath{\ell(I,x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|_2} with tolerance \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon>0}. Any theorem for squared gradient norms must first be converted to this norm scale.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Resource accounting}


Each scalar function value or noisy observation costs \AtlasInlineMath{1} call. Every location in a multipoint finite difference, every initialization query, and every reference observation is charged.



Only the declared oracle resource is charged. Computation and storage using existing information, together with explicitly known geometric and proximal operations, are free.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Algorithm views and success guarantees}


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Deterministic}


Only deterministic strategies are allowed. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.



Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.



After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The requirement \AtlasInlineMath{\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon} holds deterministically for each instance.



Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: \AtlasInlineMath{N\le T} on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.



\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Randomized}


Private randomization is allowed, with the seed independent of the instance and external randomness. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.



Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.



After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The error requirement is \AtlasInlineMath{\Pr(\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon)\ge2/3}.



Probability is over the algorithm's random seed only.



Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: \AtlasInlineMath{N\le T} on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.



\textbf{Output qualification.} Random selection among previously queried points is permitted, subject to the declared success guarantee.

Deterministic central\char45{}difference descent with a fixed cap


\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Native field: body}


Native pointer: /proofs/0/body; canonical SHA-256: d54e55ee1cc43fb2ddb5bf6d\allowbreak{}39089fe9b06e0337c6e0ae45\allowbreak{}9c79ab8a6390c635


The deterministic upper is \$O(d(1+\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta/\textbackslash{}varepsilon\textasciicircum{}2))\$, and is therefore admissible in a view allowing randomization.

At a point \$x\$, take central differences in all coordinates with \$h=\textbackslash{}varepsilon/(2\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}sqrt d)\$. Integrating the gradient Lipschitz inequality over the segment gives coordinate error at most \$\textbackslash{}beta h/2\$, so \$\textbackslash{}|g\char45{}\textbackslash{}nabla f(x)\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}varepsilon/4\$. If \$\textbackslash{}|g\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le3\textbackslash{}varepsilon/4\$, return \$x\$. Otherwise, \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x)\textbackslash{}|>\textbackslash{}varepsilon/2\$. With \$e=g\char45{}\textbackslash{}nabla f(x)\$, a step \$x\textasciicircum{}+=x\char45{}g/\textbackslash{}beta\$ obeys
\$\$f(x\textasciicircum{}+)\textbackslash{}le f(x)\char45{}\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}nabla f(x)\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\char45{}\textbackslash{}|e\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\}\{2\textbackslash{}beta\allowbreak{}\}<f(x)\char45{}\textbackslash{}frac\{3\textbackslash{}varepsilo\allowbreak{}n\textasciicircum{}2\}\{32\textbackslash{}beta\}.\$\$
More than \$32\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta/(3\textbackslash{}varepsilon\textasciicircum{}2)\$ nonterminating steps contradict the gap budget. Thus at most \$\textbackslash{}lceil32\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta/(3\textbackslash{}\allowbreak{}varepsilon\textasciicircum{}2)\textbackslash{}rceil+1\$ approximate gradients suffice, each using \$2d\$ scalar values. The finite step and stopping test provide a worst\char45{}case cap.

The separately registered randomized directional upper is the exact\char45{}noise specialization of Ghadimi and Lan\char39{}s Section 3. Its target expected squared gradient norm is expressed at the profile\char39{}s norm scale by replacing the source tolerance with a constant multiple of \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon\textasciicircum{}2\$; a finite positive smoothing radius controls its bias. That randomized witness is retained as such, rather than relabeled because a deterministic algorithm has the same leading rate.

Native pointer: /proofs/1/body; canonical SHA-256: 03f647ec88aa2bde8c8e1e21\allowbreak{}d0d63c08c350520743f1ecdc\allowbreak{}ecd80b6ade9a2f71


The registered lower bounds follow by exact simulation or class containment, with no added dimension factor.

For identical stochastic samples or identical finite\char45{}sum components, use the same exact\char45{}value hard function for every label. The oracle response is then exactly one source value, so the source\char39{}s computational lower bound transfers one\char45{}for\char45{}one. When the target observes fresh additive Gaussian values, an exact\char45{}value algorithm can generate the independent Gaussian perturbations itself; an algorithm for that noisier interface would therefore contradict the stronger exact\char45{}value lower. The exact\char45{}value source cap \$B=\textbackslash{}min\textbackslash{}\{\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta,L\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}\}\$ and its high\char45{}dimensional window remain in force. A smooth\char45{}only class may choose the proof\char45{}only budget \$L=\textbackslash{}sqrt\{\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta\}\$ inside the hard subclass; this does not add a public Lipschitz parameter.

The second\char45{}moment sample class is contained in each \$r\$\char45{}moment class for \$1<r\textbackslash{}le2\$, by \$(\textbackslash{}mathbb EG\textasciicircum{}r)\textasciicircum{}\{1/r\}\textbackslash{}le(\textbackslash{}mathbb EG\textasciicircum{}2)\textasciicircum{}\{1/2\}\$. Thus the source Goldstein statistical lower transfers to the larger heavy\char45{}tail class, but it does not establish a matching heavy\char45{}tail exponent. A composite class that includes \$\textbackslash{}psi=0\$ contains the corresponding noncomposite hard family. With \$X=\textbackslash{}mathbb R\textasciicircum{}d\$, the normal\char45{}cone residual is the unconstrained Goldstein residual. These embeddings support the registered composite and constrained\char45{}normal\char45{}cone lower bounds only where those model members are allowed; they do not automatically support a compact\char45{}set Frank\char45{}\char45{}Wolfe\char45{}gap lower bound.

A value\char45{}and\char45{}gradient incremental oracle can simulate a selected\char45{}component value by discarding the gradient. Dense26 Theorem 3.1 consequently transfers its \$\textbackslash{}Omega(n+\textbackslash{}sqrt n\textbackslash{},\textbackslash{}beta\textbackslash{}Delta/\textbackslash{}varepsilon\textasciicircum{}2)\$ lower, with \$n\textbackslash{}ge1024\$ and the registered dimension window. The same stronger\char45{}oracle ordering transfers the Hessian\char45{}Lipschitz and higher\char45{}order\char45{}smooth first\char45{}order lower theorems to exact values. A second\char45{}order stationary output necessarily satisfies its first\char45{}order gradient requirement, so the first\char45{}order lower also limits that stronger task. If the theorem states that some sufficiently large finite dimension is hard, retain \$\textbackslash{}sup\_\{d\textbackslash{}ge1\}N\textasciicircum{}*(d,\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\$ or its explicit hard\char45{}dimension bound; do not present it as a result for every fixed \$d\$.
